data.title: Trump offers first comments on Lindsay Clancy case
data.description:
President Trump responded on Friday to a judge’s decision to declare a mistrial in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial, weighing in for the first time on the legal battle that has captured national attention. 

“It’s a shame. It’s a horrible tragedy,” the president said when asked about Clancy’s case during an executive order signing ceremony in the Oval Office. 

The jury remained deadlocked on Friday after hearing five weeks of testimony and deliberating for seven days over whether to hold Clancy criminally responsible for killing her three young children in 2023. After Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial, her defense team tried and failed to appeal the decision — leading to jurors’ dismissal.

The defense argued the Massachusetts mother was experiencing postpartum psychosis when she fatally strangled her three young children, making her unable to be held criminally responsible for their deaths. The prosecution claimed she acted methodologically while killing her kids — waiting for her husband to leave the house before committing the murders.

In a Friday note to Sullivan, the jurors wrote, “It is with a heavy heart we are still unable to come to a decision and will not be able to.”

The note came a day after Clancy’s lawyers requested the removal of a holdout juror who they said refused to follow the judge’s instructions.

“It’s a terrible situation,” Trump told reporters. “Look, she did a horrible, horrible thing. Can’t be worse, but you’ll find out what the price to pay is. There’ll be a price. It’s going to be mental institution or jail or something, but I guess they’re going to go through another trial. It’s too bad.”

The prosecution now has the option to retry the case in front of a different jury, negotiate a plea deal or drop the charges entirely. Plymouth County District Attorney Tim Cruz said Friday the prosecution’s decision would be announced “shortly.”

Clancy will return to a psychiatric facility until a status hearing scheduled for the end of this month.

data.title: Federal judge raises 'meritless re-prosecution' in Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool hearing
data.description:
A D.C. judge peppered federal prosecutors with questions on Friday about President Trump’s recent remarks about a former Olympian accused of damaging the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, as the prosecutors sought to convince him that the possibility of future charges should be left open. 

Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman asked assistant U.S. Attorney Michael Spence how he was supposed to look at the president’s statements about Hearn, one of his attorneys and U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jeanine Pirro as “anything other than [Trump] pressuring your office, your boss and the three of you to charge Mr. Hearn, recharge Mr. Hearn with what you had decided to be a meritless prosecution.” 

“Isn’t this a unique threat of meritless re-prosecution?” Edelman said. 

Spence replied only that Trump’s statements “speak for themselves,” while also arguing that it was premature to discuss that hypothetical notion because no further grand jury action had happened. 

The exchange came during a hearing to decide whether a case against David Hearn should be dismissed for good after the U.S. attorney’s office backed away from the case due to insufficient evidence to support felony charges. 

That move drew the ire of Trump, who bashed Pirro on multiple occassions as he urged her to reconsider. 

“She folded like an umbrella,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Aug. 3, saying the U.S. attorney had “choked.” It was rare public break between the two usually friendly allies, leaving Pirro’s job security in limbo. 

Trump later lashed out at Hearn, referencing the former Olympic canoeist’s prior donations to Democrats through the ActBlue fundraising platform. 

“A National Park Service career employee, a highly credible witness, saw David Hearn (ActBlue) in broad daylight vandalize the Reflecting Pool by ‘violently’ ripping and tugging at the Pool’s somewhat delicate coating,” the president wrote in an Aug. 9 post on Truth Social. 

Hearn was charged with felony destruction of property in early July after prosecutors alleged that they had enough evidence to prove that he had “willfully damaged” the landmark by ripping up a piece of sealant. He initially pleaded not guilty and was scheduled to go to trial at the end of this month. 

But several weeks later, Pirro’s office conceded that a flawed and rushed installation by a no-bid contractor, not vandalism, was likely responsible for the peeling paint.

Prosecutors blamed the Interior Department for failing to hand over complete information before the case was presented to a grand jury and moved to dismiss the charges. 

Edelman granted that request in early August but deferred a decision on whether prosecutors should be allowed to try to charge Hearn again at a later date. Hearn’s attorneys have asked that the case be dismissed with prejudice, meaning it would be closed for good. 

“Why are they reserving the right to reindict a case they acknowledge should never have been indicted?” one of Hearn’s lawyers, Steve Levin, told the judge. He said there was “no legitimate purpose” to keep the prosecution alive. 

Soon after the more than $14 million remodel of the reflecting pool was completed in early June, chunks of the “American flag blue” coating hand-picked by Trump began peeling and floating to the water’s surface.

The president quickly blamed the issues on vandalism, alleging that detractors had intentionally cut a lengthy slit into the lining. But court filings indicate that a National Park Service engineer warned within days of the installation that the “top layer of the liner has peeled.”

Edelman did not issue a ruling from the bench, saying only that the parties should expect to hear from him soon.

data.title: What to know about latest Missouri redistricting ruling
data.description:
The Missouri Supreme Court delivered a last-minute twist in the midterm’s redistricting saga this week when the predominantly Republican governor-appointed court ruled that new maps passed by state lawmakers to give their party an extra seat couldn’t immediately go into effect. 

Instead, the high court said, the coalition looking to temporarily stall the new GOP-favored 7-1 House map from being used in this year’s elections met the requirements to have the new congressional lines put to a referendum in November. That would mean the state would then be using its Republican-leaning 6-2 map in November. 

The new ruling injects uncertainty into Missouri’s elections given that the state held their primaries using the new GOP-favored 7-1 House map in last month’s primaries. The Missouri attorney general’s office has already said they intend to appeal the decision to the U.S. Supreme Court.  

Here’s a quick rundown on what to know about the latest Missouri redistricting ruling: 

Missouri court wants old maps in place

The Show Me State has been swept up in a broader redistricting war as Republicans looked to redraw congressional lines across the country to net pickup opportunities ahead of November, with Democrats responding in kind.  

Missouri Republicans faced pressure from President Trump and national Republicans to redraw their House map from its current delegation makeup of six Republicans and two Democrats to a new map that could create a 7-1 edge for the GOP. The new map seeks to weaken Rep. Emanuel Cleaver’s (D-Mo.) Kansas City-based seat. 

GOP lawmakers passed the new map last fall, prompting opponents to find a way to stall the new lines. 

A coalition called People Not Politicians are pushing for a referendum on the November ballot that asks voters whether or not to approve the new 7-1 House map. But Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins (R) made a late decision that the measure couldn’t be placed on the ballot, arguing the state Constitution doesn’t permit state legislature-led congressional redistricting to go before voters, among other reasons. 

The Missouri high court rejected the GOP secretary’s arguments in a notably unanimous 7-0 decision — five of the justices were appointed by a Republican governor — by writing, “Because the referendum petition was legal, sufficient, and timely, [the new House map] never took effect and was referred to the voters as of December 9, 2025.” 

“The congressional districts the General Assembly established in 2022 remain in full force and effect for the November 2026 general election, and [the new House map] will not take effect unless and until approved by the voters at the November 2026 general election,” the court added. 

Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway (R) immediately said the state would be escalating the issue to the U.S. Supreme Court. Meanwhile, the Missouri Supreme Court declined Hoskins’s request to halt the high court’s new ruling on the map as the state makes their appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court. 

New ruling creates headaches for candidates

The ruling creates some headaches for congressional primary winners given that Missouri already held their contests last month and relied on the Republican redistricted maps. 

People Not Politicians attorney Chuck Hatfield suggested that the winners of last month’s primaries would head to the general election in November, or that political parties can decide on their own nominees, according to St. Louis Public Radio.  

The Hill has reached out to Hoskins’s office for guidance on how the ruling impacts the state’s primaries.  

The last few states — New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Delaware — are wrapping up their primaries this month, with Election Day roughly 60 days out. Undergoing a new primary — let alone voter education — could be intensive, costly and challenging. 

Missouri GOP turns to U.S. Supreme Court for help

Missouri Republicans hadn’t officially issued their appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court at time of publication, though observers expect that Republicans will argue that lawmakers have the authority to redistrict under the U.S. Constitution.  

Several legal experts that spoke to the Missouri Independent say it’s unlikely Republicans will be able to successfully appeal to the country’s highest court.  

The U.S. Supreme Court declined Virginia Democrats’ appeal in May to have their more Democratic-friendly 9-2 map used in time for the general election after the state’s highest court struck the effort down. Instead, Virginia held its primaries under the current 6-5 Democratic edge House map. 

Redistricting math changes very little

The back-of-the-napkin redistricting math is expected to change little after the Missouri Supreme Court’s ruling given that Republicans only changed their congressional lines to pick up one additional seat in the lower chamber. 

For Democrats, the redistricting ruling is a win because it means Cleaver will likely return to Congress — his seat went for former Vice President Harris in 2024 by 23 points.  

While Republicans have been able to successfully redraw more House seats in their favor in Texas, Ohio, North Carolina, Florida, Louisiana, Alabama and Tennessee compared to Democrats’ expected gains in California and Utah, election forecasts expect Democrats to flip the lower chamber in November.  

Decision Desk HQ forecasts that Democrats have a 67 percent chance of taking back the House compared to a 33 percent chance of Republicans holding it.

data.title: Lancaster County, PA infant confirmed to have died from measles
data.description:
A six-week-old infant’s death in Pennsylvania was caused by measles, the Lancaster County coroner confirmed Friday.

County coroner Stephen Diamantoni said the child, who died last month, was born with Amish lethal microcephaly, a rare genetic condition that can cause respiratory infections.

Pennsylvania health officials last week announced the “measles-related” deaths of two unvaccinated people, including an infant, as the state grapples with an outbreak that has sickened 577 people and hospitalized 98 as of Friday.

Their deaths were the first measles-related deaths in the state in 35 years and the first in the U.S. this year.

It has not been confirmed if the six-week-old child was one of the previously-announced two cases.

At the time, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention did not confirm whether measles was the cause of death in both cases.

“Available information does not establish whether measles caused or contributed to the deaths or whether the individuals died from other causes while infected with measles,” the CDC’s website read. “CDC will update the national count as additional information becomes available.”

Diamantoni said in an interview with Lancaster Online, which first reported details of the child’s death, that his office began to investigate the second case after the announcement from state health officials.

After learning of the child’s Amish lethal microcephaly diagnosis and reviewing her medical records, he said he was able to confirm that the cause of death was measles.

According to Diamantoni, the clinic that was treating the child did not initially report the case to the coroner because the child’s death was not surprising. Children diagnosed with that genetic condition often die within months of birth from viral respiratory illnesses.

“The child did test positive for measles. We know that children with this disorder will die of respiratory infections,” Diamantoni said. “Measles is a respiratory infection and we know the life expectancy of these poor kids is very short.”

Trump administration officials, including Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., have questioned Pennsylvania’s handling of the measles outbreak, publicly feuding with Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) over transparency.

“We don’t know exactly what happened in Pennsylvania yet,” Dr. Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, said in an interview with Fox Business.

“We don’t know if the children died from measles or had another condition that was already attacking them and they happened to get measles at the same time.”

data.title: Trump says data center opponents face 'poverty, crime and squalor'
data.description:
President Trump took aim at data center opponents again Friday, suggesting they want to “go through poverty, crime and squalor.”

It marks the second time this week that Trump has gone after critics of AI infrastructure, which has become increasingly unpopular among Americans in recent months.

“If you want to get rich as a state or as a town, if you want to pay lower taxes, if you want to create tremendous wealth, if you want your house to be more valuable and everything else, you’re going to want a data center,” Trump said after an unrelated signing in the Oval Office.

“If you want to go through poverty, crime and squalor, I would say don’t approve data centers,” he continued. “You know, you have your choice. So I’m all for people approving them or not.”

The president similarly suggested in a Truth Social post on Monday that the “only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor.”

He has long embraced the push to build more data centers across the country, an endeavor that tech companies argue is necessary to support AI development.

But Americans have grown wary of such projects over concerns they could result in higher electricity costs, strain water resources and produce noise or air pollution.

While data centers have brought in greater tax revenue for some communities, numerous jurisdictions used tax breaks to attract the investments. States including Ohio and Illinois have paused such tax incentive programs in recent months, while others have moved even more aggressively, with New York instituting the nation’s first statewide freeze on new “hyperscale” data centers.

Trump’s comments come as Democrats and Republicans alike have sought to distance themselves from the server warehouses powering the AI boom, which are increasingly become a central issue in the midterm elections.

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D), who once touted new Amazon data centers in the Keystone State, announced new restrictions on development last month, as he faced attacks on the issue from his Republican opponent.

Former Rep. Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee for Senate in Michigan, has called for a one-year moratorium on new data center projects, and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) paused data center construction pending state audits.

data.title: Live updates: August's strong jobs numbers put rate cut in doubt; Trump signs beef deal
data.description:
The U.S. economy added 162,000 jobs last month, a stronger-than-expected showing. And now President Trump wants to see interest rates dropped, threatening to cut off trade with several countries if the Federal Reserve doesn’t budge at its September meeting.

“Without the United States agreeing to allow them their big surpluses, and we could stop that immediately, they would no longer be considered financially ELITE!” he wrote on Truth Social. “LOWER THE RATE OR I’LL STOP TRADING WITH COUNTRIES WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT.”

On Friday afternoon, Trump signed an executive order allowing tariff-free imported beef, coming from Brazil and Argentina, among other places, as his administration works to alleviate stubbornly high prices.

The judge in the Lindsay Clancy murder case announced Friday that he was declaring a mistrial after jurors were unable to reach a unanimous verdict. However, when defense attorney Kevin Reddington requested an immediate stay of the declaration, the judge gave the defense one hour to appeal.

North Carolina is set to begin mailing general election absentee ballots Friday, even as the Trump administration has moved to restrict voting by mail.

The administration is appealing a federal judge’s ruling that stops it from moving forward with voting restrictions established by executive order for at least for one more week. The Justice Department asked the Supreme Court on Thursday to lift the block.

Trump had a policy meeting and will sign an executive order Friday before heading to New Jersey for the holiday weekend.

Follow along live below.

data.title: Trump signs controversial beef deal with Brazil, Argentina
data.description:
President Trump said Friday that tariff-free imported beef will be coming from Brazil and Argentina, among other places, as his administration works to alleviate stubbornly high prices.

“It’s coming from Argentina. It’s coming from Brazil,” Trump said at an Oval Office event surrounded by ranchers and farmers. “It’s coming from a couple of other places. We have our inspectors down. It’s very clean. It’s very good.”

Trump announced last month that the U.S. would be pausing tariffs on 300,000 metric tons of beef for 90 days to be sold at a 25 percent discount below market price. The president said it would lower costs for Americans while allowing for ranchers to build up their herds.

The announcement was quickly criticized by the cattle industry and GOP lawmakers who said that lowering prices for Americans shouldn’t come at the cost of U.S. ranchers.

“We’re doing it in a very limited fashion because our ranchers can handle it, but our ranchers really needed a little bit of help, and our ranchers want the prices to be down, too,” Trump said.

The White House further defended the decision after a report that a Brazilian billionaire influenced it. The Wall Street Journal reported Monday that Trump met with Joesley Batisa, who shares control of JBS, the world’s largest meatpacker, a day before the announcement.

Batista and his brother Wesley Batista were fined in 2020 by the Justice Department over charges that they violated the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act by using funds obtained through a bribery scheme to expand operations in the U.S.

The tariff pause also follows the unrelated recall of nearly 30,000 pounds of Argentinian beef that had been distributed in Texas and Florida.

Trump was behind the Resolute Desk Friday to sign two executive orders, one that allows ranchers and farmers to butcher, process, package and sell their own products and another that requires country-of-origin labeling across all foreign beef.

Trump said the big four processors in the U.S. beef sector — Tyson Foods, JBS S.A., Cargill and National Beef Packing Co. — have a “monopoly” on the industry.

“I’ve heard all about it. I’ve been listening to it… and they say they’re a very nasty group, very difficult to deal with,” he said of the processors. “And they cost our farmers a lot of money, and they cost our ranchers a lot of money, and they cost the public a lot of money in grief, and we’re not going to let it happen any longer.”

When asked about the timeline on the country-of-origin labeling, Trump said he would need to go through Capitol Hill.

“We’re putting it in front of Congress right away,” he said. “It should be no problem.”

data.title: Supreme Court sides with GOP in fight over TV ad rates; Jackson dissents
data.description:
The Supreme Court on Friday lifted a ruling that prevented party committees from accessing cheaper advertising rates in the lead-up to November’s elections, siding with Republicans, for now, in an emergency case that drew staunch Democratic opposition.

Federal law mandates that broadcast stations offer their lowest available rate in the 60 days preceding a general election. Everyone agrees candidates get the discount, but whether political parties and joint fundraising committees can, too, has come under question.

The court appeared to split 8-1, though the justices don’t have to disclose their votes in emergency decisions publicly. The majority said that federal courts had no authority yet to intervene in the dispute.

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, the court’s junior liberal justice, publicly dissented.

Republicans’ Senate and House campaign arms — boasting a cash advantage and backed by the Trump administration — brought the fight to the Supreme Court after Democrats sued to stop them from accessing the cheaper rate.

Democrats won before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit. In a 2-1 decision, the panel ruled the Federal Communications Commission’s (FCC) notice asserting the committees could enjoy the discount wasn’t legal.

In their Supreme Court filings, Republicans largely centered their case on the notion that the judges had no authority to get involved, describing the notice as a “staff-level guidance document.”

“The decision opens the floodgates, allowing challenges to staff decisions of the FCC and other agencies in parallel tracks before the Commission and courts,” they wrote in court filings.

Republicans’ emergency appeal garnered support from the Trump administration, which similarly told the high court the lower courts had no authority.

“The challengers claim, and the court of appeals agreed, that the notice injures them by making it cheaper for their opponents to run campaign advertisements,” Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote to the justices. “But the notice does not grant favored treatment to one side or the other; instead, the notice’s interpretation offers the same benefit to all sides”

Democrats insisted to the justices the lower courts acted properly and had power to intervene.

“On both reviewability and the merits, Applicants and the United States want to talk about everything except the text of the directly pertinent statutes. That is because on both questions, the text directly supports Candidates,” they wrote in court filings.

data.title: 4 House Democrats heading to Dallas for RNC counterprogramming
data.description:
Four House Democrats are headed to Dallas next week as the Republican National Committee holds a first-of-its-kind midterm convention, House leadership announced on Friday. 

Reps. Robert Garcia, (D-Calif.), Jason Crow (D-Colo.), Madeleine Dean (D-Pa.) and Sydney Kamlager-Dove (D-Calif.) make up the delegation, which will partner with local leaders and the Texas Democratic Party on the ground. 

“While swing seat House Republicans try to hide from their record of raising costs on working families, gutting Medicaid to fund tax breaks for billionaire donors and supporting a reckless war of choice in Iran, House Democrats will be present to hold them accountable,” House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) said in a release. 

Jeffries accused MAGA extremists of “partying with their super rich donors in Dallas” as Americans feel the sting of high prices.

“Americans are being crushed by rising costs. Republicans don’t care—they’re in Dallas, celebrating an out of touch President whose tariffs and wars are making things worse. We’re going to hold them accountable,” Crow said on X.

The Democrats’ Texas visit acts as a counterprogramming to the RNC’s convention, which is aimed at highlighting Republican candidates and energizing the party’s voters ahead of the high-stakes midterm election. Vice President Vance is giving a speech the first night, and President Trump is set to deliver the closing-night keynote address. 

The Dallas-based event comes as Republicans fight to hold on to the Texas Senate seat up for grabs in November, and as both parties battle over a handful of highly competitive House seats after GOP-friendly redistricting reshaped the state’s congressional maps last year.

data.title: Virginia Democrat says DOJ wiretapped phone calls with state Senate leader
data.description:
Rep. Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.) said Thursday that the FBI and Justice Department (DOJ) informed him they had wiretapped his past phone conversations with a Virginia state lawmaker.

Subramanyam’s office shared photos of two letters he said he received from the agencies, dated from July and August, notifying him they monitored some of his calls with Virginia state Senate President Pro Tempore Louise Lucas (D).

The representative slammed this action as “deeply concerning” in his Thursday statement, accusing the Trump administration of trying to intimidate Democrats.

A federal judge authorized the phone call interception in April, according to the letters. A month later, federal agents conducted a search of Lucas’ office and a cannabis dispensary she co-owned as part of this investigation. The state legislator has denied any wrongdoing and claimed the federal probe was politically motivated. 

Subramanyam’s statement described called the timing of the phone tapping and investigation into the Virginia state senate leader “extremely suspicious.”

He noted the probe occurred within the same period Virginia Democrats were pushing for a redistricting referendum — an effort that Lucas championed.

The Virginia representative also pointed to his role on the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform as a potential reason for the agencies’ scrutiny, noting he and other Democrats were demanding answers from the DOJ at the time over its handling of the investigation into late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

“This should concern anyone who believes in a real Department of Justice that serves the American people and not a singular president,” Subramanyam said.

“If this surveillance was done to scare us and to get Democrats to stop pushing back against [President] Trump’s political overreach, they are mistaken,” he continued. “We will not back down. We will continue our investigations into this President and his corrupt administration.”  

The Hill has reached out to the DOJ and Lucas for comment. The FBI declined to comment.
